stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Arctic terns make one of the longest migrations of any animal, traveling each year between Arctic breeding grounds and Antarctic waters. Tracking data collected from birds tagged on small islands off the coast of ______ that a single tern can cover tens of thousands of kilometers in one year, zigzagging across the Atlantic to ride favorable winds.
explanation: The subject is the long phrase "Tracking data collected from birds tagged on small islands off the coast of Greenland," and its verb is "show." Nothing should separate a subject from its verb, however long the subject is, so you leave out punctuation entirely.

A.why: You added a comma because the subject is long and you wanted a pause. A comma can't sit between a subject and its verb, so this splits "data" from "show."

C.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side. "Tracking data ... off the coast of Greenland" has no verb, so it's a fragment.

D.why: A colon needs a complete sentence before it. Everything before the colon is only a subject with no verb, so the colon can't go there.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Small earthquakes can reveal the hidden shape of a fault. Over a three-month study in the foothills of the Varden Range, a network of seismometers buried along the fault ______ of tiny tremors, most far too faint for nearby residents to feel. Mapping where those tremors began let the team trace the fault's path underground.
explanation: "Recorded" is the verb and "thousands of tiny tremors" is its direct object. A verb and its object run straight together with no punctuation.

A.why: You treated the object as a list the sentence was introducing. A colon can't split a verb from its object; "a network of seismometers ... recorded" doesn't finish the thought on its own.

B.why: You put a comma where it felt like a breath pause after the verb. Commas don't separate a verb from its object.

D.why: A semicolon joins two complete sentences, but "thousands of tiny tremors, most far too faint..." has no main verb of its own, so it's a fragment.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Carving a woodblock is only half of the printmaker's craft. In her workshop manual, artist Ines Varga explains how to roll ink across the block in a thin, even ______ how to lift the paper away without smudging the finest carved lines. Both steps, she argues, take longer to master than the carving itself.
explanation: "And" joins two parallel objects of "explains": "how to roll ink..." and "how to lift the paper...." Neither one is an independent clause, so no punctuation goes before "and."

B.why: You added a comma before "and" as if it joined two sentences. It only joins two "how to" phrases, and a comma shouldn't split a pair like that.

C.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence after it. "And how to lift the paper away..." is a fragment.

D.why: A colon would mark the second "how to" phrase as an explanation of the first. It is actually the second half of a coordinated pair, so the colon breaks up that pair.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Each spring, the reservoir behind the Pellan Dam loses storage capacity as sediment washes in from upstream. By sampling water from every stream in the basin, hydrologists identified the single ______ nearly a third of that sediment: a short, steep creek draining a recently logged hillside.
explanation: "That carries nearly a third of that sediment" is an essential clause. It tells you which tributary the hydrologists identified. An essential "that" clause attaches directly to its noun with no punctuation.

A.why: You set off the "that" clause with a comma as if it were extra information. It's needed to identify the tributary, and a comma never comes before an essential "that" clause.

B.why: A colon needs a complete sentence before it. "Hydrologists identified the single tributary" leaves the object without the clause that defines it, so the colon splits a noun from its identifying clause.

C.why: A dash cuts the noun off from the essential clause that identifies it, just as a comma would. Nothing should go between "tributary" and "that."

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: To make its downtown safer for cyclists, the city of Ardmore redesigned Harlow Avenue in 2022. The project narrowed the avenue's four car lanes to ______ protected bike lanes on both sides of the street, separated from traffic by a row of concrete planters.
explanation: "The project" is the subject of two verbs, "narrowed" and "added," joined by "and." The second verb has no subject of its own, so this is one clause with a compound verb, and no punctuation belongs before "and."

A.why: You added a comma before "and" as if a second complete sentence followed. "And added protected bike lanes" has no subject, so the comma splits a pair of verbs that belong together.

C.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence after it, and "and added protected bike lanes..." has no subject.

D.why: You dropped the "and" and left only a comma between the two verbs. That leaves "narrowed..." and "added..." awkwardly spliced together with nothing joining them.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Mantis shrimp—reef-dwelling crustaceans rarely longer than a human hand—hunt with a pair of club-shaped appendages folded beneath their heads. The force that these clubs deliver in a single ______ enough to shatter a snail's shell or even crack the glass of an aquarium tank.
explanation: The subject is "The force that these clubs deliver in a single strike," and the verb is "is." Once you see the subject–verb relationship, you know nothing goes between them. The essential clause "that these clubs deliver..." is part of the subject too.

A.why: You paused after the long subject with a comma. A comma can't separate a subject from its verb, even when the subject is long.

B.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side. "The force that these clubs deliver in a single strike" has no main verb, so it's a fragment.

C.why: A colon needs a complete sentence before it. What comes before the colon is only a subject, and its verb, "is," comes after.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Coaches have long suspected that sleep affects athletic performance, and a recent study offers support. After tracking twenty-four college sprinters for six weeks, researchers at the Halvorsen Sports Institute ______ athletes who slept at least nine hours a night ran their 60-meter trials measurably faster than those who slept less.
explanation: The clause "that athletes who slept at least nine hours... ran... faster" is the direct object of "found." It tells you what the researchers found. A verb runs straight into its object with no punctuation.

B.why: You put a comma where you'd pause before a long result. Commas don't separate a verb from its object, and the whole "that" clause is the object of "found."

C.why: A colon needs a complete sentence before it. "Researchers ... found" leaves the verb without the object it needs, so the colon cuts the verb off from what it takes.

D.why: A single dash works like a colon, so it has the same problem: it separates "found" from its object, the clause stating what was found.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Farmers in the region have debated whether composted manure can replace synthetic fertilizer without shrinking their harvests. In a four-year field trial, agronomist Priya Natarajan compared the yields of wheat plots treated with synthetic ______ yields of plots treated only with compost; the difference between the two was less than 3 percent.
explanation: "Compared" takes two parallel objects joined by "and": "the yields of wheat plots treated with synthetic fertilizer" and "the yields of plots treated only with compost." Two coordinated noun phrases need no punctuation between them.

A.why: The first noun phrase is long, so you added a comma before "and." But "and" joins two objects of "compared," not two sentences, so no comma belongs there.

B.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side. "And the yields of plots treated only with compost" has no verb, so it's a fragment.

D.why: A colon would present the second group of yields as an explanation of the first. They're really the two things being compared, and the colon breaks that pair apart.
